text: Enkidu Enters the City: Why Growth Always Comes with Loss
Enkidu first lives in the wilderness.

His body is covered in hair. He grazes with the animals and drinks beside them at the water. He dismantles the hunter's traps and lets the animals escape. To the people of the city, he is both powerful and difficult to fit into the existing order.
Unable to deal with him, the hunter goes for help.
A woman named Shamhat is brought into the wilderness. Her time with Enkidu changes his life.
When Enkidu later tries to return to the herds, the animals avoid him. He can no longer keep up with them as he once did.
At the same time, he gains new understanding.
Shamhat says to him: You are different now. Why keep roaming with the beasts? Come to Uruk. People practice all kinds of crafts there, and Gilgamesh is there too.
Enkidu accepts the invitation.
He eats human food, puts on clothes, joins other people and hears about the city. Later, when he learns how Gilgamesh intends to use his power, he stands in his way to stop him.
They fight, then become friends.
From then on, Enkidu has relationships, language, possibilities for action and glory he never had in the wilderness.
Nor does he ever return to his former life.
This story is easily told as “a wild man becomes civilized.”
In that version, the wilderness stands for ignorance and the city for growth. Shamhat leads Enkidu out of the animal world into truly human life; every loss is merely the price progress must pay.
It can also be reversed into another familiar story:
A person once free and whole is seduced and tamed by the city, loses his connection with nature, and is finally drawn into a hero's ambitions and dies as a result.
Both versions grasp part of the facts.
Both are too quick.
The text gives Enkidu neither gains alone nor losses alone.
The animals' departure is real.
The new understanding is real too.
He loses an old world while entering, for the first time, one in which he can speak, judge, oppose and make friends.
Choose only one side, and the story's real difficulty disappears.
Growth is often imagined as addition.
Knowing how to do more, seeing farther, gaining entry to more places and having more choices.
But much growth does not simply add a capacity to the self we already are.
It changes that self, making some old relationships impossible.
When a child learns to explain themselves in new language, relationships once sustained only by cries and screams will change.
When someone enters a new world of knowledge, answers that once explained life sufficiently may no longer suffice.
Once someone truly develops their own judgment, they may no longer be able to return unconditionally to the safety of needing only to obey.
As we gain new capacities, we also lose some old ignorance, dependence and belonging.
These losses do not necessarily prove growth wrong.
But they cannot be treated as though they never happened simply because growth brings more capacities.
Enkidu approaching the herds and the herds fleeing is one of this story's clearest marks.
Change has entered the body and its relationships.
Even if he regrets it immediately, a decision alone cannot take him back to before the change.
This makes “did he consent to change?” a question with no easy answer.

Shamhat's arrival was arranged by others. The hunter and the city wanted to deal with a being who obstructed the order of hunting. Enkidu did not volunteer to enter civilization after fully understanding the consequences.
Yet neither is he an object passively transported into the city.
After the animals leave and his understanding grows, he listens to the invitation and starts toward Uruk. Nor does he later enter the city merely to become the worker it needs.
One of his first important acts is to stop Gilgamesh.
This matters enormously.
If an education or guidance merely makes someone more willing to obey the existing order, it may increase only the order's ability to use them.
Enkidu's new capacities, however, let him judge the city and stand before its strongest man to say no.
The city has not simply made him one of its components.
It has given him a position in life from which he can question the city in return.
At least at this moment, external change has not completely prescribed his direction.
But this still does not make the process wholly justified or free of harm.
Shamhat's guidance changes him, and Enkidu bears most of the cost.
The animals do not join the discussion.
The old world does not speak in its own defense.
Nor can Enkidu, before the change, use understanding gained only afterward to assess in advance what he will lose.
This is precisely the difficulty every relationship of growth encounters.
Someone who does not yet possess a capacity cannot decide entirely from within that capacity whether to acquire it.
Before learning language, a child cannot use mature language to choose whether to learn it.
Someone who has never entered a field of knowledge cannot know in advance how it will change their view.
If every change must await the consent of an already fully formed decision-maker, many processes that form the capacity to decide cannot even begin.
Yet if “this is to help you grow” is sufficient to justify intervention, helpers acquire almost unlimited power.
The story does not resolve this contradiction for us.
It only makes the criteria of judgment more demanding.
We cannot ask only whether the change began from outside.

We must also ask: Afterward, has this person gained richer capacities for judgment and action? Can they use those new capacities to oppose their guide, alter their course, even leave the world that gave them those capacities?
And we must ask: Which old possibilities have closed? Have those losses been seen, or do they no longer count simply because the victors call it progress?
Enkidu later travels far.
He develops a deep friendship with Gilgamesh, helps kill Humbaba, then kills the Bull of Heaven. From an opponent of the city, he becomes a partner in heroic undertakings.
This path brings him glory and also leads him toward death.
In the account of his final days, he briefly curses the hunter and Shamhat, as though all his calamities came from that first step away from the wilderness.
Then, reminded by a god, he withdraws his curse on Shamhat and blesses her instead: she gave him food, clothes and a place in the city, and brought him to Gilgamesh.
This reversal is crucial.
If the story retained only the curse, we could write entry into city life as pure degeneration.
If it retained only the blessing, we could count the loss of the wilderness entirely as a reasonable cost for friendship and glory.
But Enkidu's life contains both.
Entering the human world did give him an irreplaceable friendship.
Entering that world also drew him into the conflicts and pursuit of glory that would kill him.
As he dies, he cannot settle the account of his life with one simple conclusion.
Nor should we do it for him.
People often say every choice has a price.
Sometimes this merely serves to make loss seem beyond further question.
As though acknowledging a gain automatically justified every cost.
But costs can be necessary or avoidable, chosen by the person or arranged for them by others, proportionate to what is gained or concealed afterward behind those gains.
Enkidu's story reminds us:
Growth having a price does not mean every loss inflicted in its name is justified.
Equally, growth changing the former self does not make the new self unreal.
Someone cannot conclude that every later wish was merely implanted by others just because they have been influenced from outside.
If so, almost no direction in the world would belong to anyone, since all our languages, capacities and imaginable paths have reached us through others.
What truly belongs to a person need not be something untouched by influence.
It can also be something they judge anew after the influence, continue to take responsibility for, and use to act in ways others have not scripted beforehand.
After entering the city, Enkidu does not merely become who Shamhat or Gilgamesh wants him to be.
He opposes, chooses, loves and makes mistakes.
That life is already his.
Precisely for that reason, its consequences become his consequences too.
Perhaps the easiest person to overlook in this story is Shamhat.
Later readings often reduce her to a temptress: she uses her body to strip Enkidu of his natural innocence.
But she has another role in the text.
She introduces Enkidu to the city, teaches him to enter human life, explains what is there, and recognizes the changes that have already taken place in him.
She is not an empty doorway.
She brings a world before him.
That certainly includes a guide's power.
She knows things Enkidu does not and helps change the life he can imagine. For that very reason, her responsibility cannot be erased entirely.
But guidance does not necessarily mean taking over.
What matters is whether the world she opens allows Enkidu to develop his own judgment afterward.
His daring to stop Gilgamesh suggests the answer is at least not wholly negative.
He learns more than how to adapt to the city.
He also learns that the city can be opposed.
Enkidu's story offers no completely safe model of growth.

There is no method that gives him language, friendship and public action while guaranteeing his wilderness relationships remain unchanged. Nor is there a choice that lets him know in advance what the city will give him and take away.
Growth here is not a steady ascent from a lower state to a higher one.
It is a door through which there is no going back.
Beyond it lie more of the world, and new dangers too.
Whoever crosses gains a self they did not have, and loses a self to which they can never return unchanged.
So genuinely mature education and help should not promise those receiving them:
You will only gain, never lose.
They should instead honestly acknowledge:
New capacities will change you; some old ways of life will close. I cannot know every cost for you in advance, nor does introducing you to the door give me ownership of your life after you enter.
What I can do is try to ensure that you gain not only the ability to adapt to the new world, but also the ability to judge, refuse and choose again within it.
After Enkidu leaves the wilderness, the animals no longer accept him.
Yet the city does not thereby become an untroubled home.
He first opposes its king, then comes to love that king and pursue glory with him, and finally, facing death, curses and blesses the person who brought him here.
No single sentence can settle all these changes.
Perhaps that is the story's most honest part.
Growth is not preserving a self entirely untouched by influence.
Nor is it letting someone else install a better self inside us.
It is gradually acquiring a new capacity after some old roads have closed:
To acknowledge that we have changed, distinguish gains from losses, and give our own answer about the road we still have to walk.
When Enkidu enters the city, he cannot know where this road will ultimately lead.
But there he is not only changed.
For the first time, he also becomes someone able to change the human world.

*Textual basis and versions: this essay follows Enkidu's transformation and entry into the city as preserved in Tablets I–II of the Standard Babylonian Epic of Gilgamesh, also consulting the corresponding passage in Old Babylonian Tablet II in which Shamhat invites Enkidu to Uruk. The deathbed curse, its withdrawal and the blessing of Shamhat come from Standard Babylonian Tablet VII. Versions differ in food, clothing, sequence of actions and wording; this essay does not treat all their details as one undifferentiated “original version.”*
